preamble: The diphthong /oi/ was monophthongized to the close front rounded vowel /y/ in post-classical Greek, probably via intermediate [øi] and [øː]. The change appears first in Boeotian (3rd century BC) and was complete in Koine by about the 1st century BC to 2nd century AD, after which /y/ merged with /i/. Outside Greek, a direct oi > y change is rarely documented; related languages more often give [ø] (as in Korean or Nagoya Japanese) or [u] (as in Latin oi > ū).

examples.note: Spellings of υ for οι and confusion of the two in Egyptian papyri from the 1st century BC show that οι had merged with υ /y/; both later became /i/.

examples.from: τοῖς ἄλλοις προξένοις 'to the other proxenoi' (Attic spelling)
examples.note: Boeotian inscriptions from the 3rd century BC write υ for οι, so the monophthongization to [yː] came early in this dialect.

sources: Allen, W. S. (1987). Vox Graeca: A Guide to the Pronunciation of Classical Greek (3rd ed.). Cambridge University Press. https://ci.nii.ac.jp/ncid/BA0124031X
